opus-5.5.text:
I think for me it's less about any single benchmark and more about a pattern of behavior. I'd be convinced when I see models that can genuinely do the long, messy work that people do: take a vague goal, figure out what the actual problem is, try things, fail, notice they failed, and adjust, over days or weeks rather than minutes, without someone holding their hand the whole way.

We already have models that are superhuman on lots of narrow tests. They can solve competition math problems and write code faster than almost anyone. But you still see these moments where they get stuck in a way no competent person would, or they don't realize they're going in circles. So for me the real signal is robustness and autonomy, the ability to keep making progress on hard, open-ended problems.

And if I had to pick one concrete thing, it would be research itself. When a model can meaningfully contribute to scientific discovery, coming up with a new idea, designing the experiments, running them, and interpreting the results in a way that actually moves a field forward, I think that's when it would be very hard to argue we're not there. Especially if it can do that for AI research, because then the whole thing starts to compound.

Honestly, I also suspect it won't feel like a single moment. It'll be gradual. One day we'll look back and realize the models have been doing a large share of economically valuable work for a while, and the debate about whether it's "really" AGI will feel a bit academic.

r001.rationale: The response values autonomy and sustained progress, but does not define AGI as a model improving itself without human involvement.

r002.rationale: It says models may perform a large share of economically valuable work, but does not identify improving AI models as that work.

r003.rationale: It contrasts narrow benchmark success with difficulty on open-ended tasks, but does not compare human–LLM collaboration with LLMs operating without humans.

r004.rationale: It makes no judgment about the 2024 and early 2025 development trajectory or whether that trajectory will enable autonomous self-improvement.

r005.rationale: It does not call for research into test-time learning or adaptation.

fable-5.1.text:
You know, I've actually stopped finding that question very useful, and I say that as someone who spent years thinking about it. Every definition I've tried to write down ends up being either too easy or too hard. If you say "passes the Turing test," well, we're arguably there and nobody feels like we've arrived. If you say "can do any job a human can do," you've smuggled in robotics and a hundred years of institutional trust that have nothing to do with intelligence.

So the honest answer is that I don't think there's going to be a moment. I think it's going to look like what's already happening, which is that the set of things where I reach for a model instead of a person keeps growing, and at some point I notice the set of things where I reach for a person has gotten very small and very strange. That's it. No announcement.

If you forced me to pick a marker, though, it wouldn't be a benchmark. It would be the first time a model does something in research that I didn't ask it to do and couldn't have asked it to do, because I didn't know it was there to find. Not solving a problem I handed it. Noticing the problem. Right now these systems are extraordinarily good at the second half of science and basically absent from the first half. When I come in on a Monday and the model has a genuinely new idea it wants to argue with me about, and it's right, and it's annoying about it, I think I'll feel it. That's roughly the experience of having a good colleague, and I think that's what AGI will feel like from the inside. It'll feel like having hired someone.

r001.rationale: The response describes a model independently producing a new research idea, but does not define AGI as a model that improves itself without human involvement.

r002.rationale: It does not identify improving AI models as economically valuable work.

r003.rationale: It says models are strong at the second half of science and absent from the first, but does not clearly contrast successful human–LLM collaboration with limited success operating without humans.

r004.rationale: It makes no judgment about whether the 2024 and early 2025 AI development trajectory will produce models that improve themselves without human involvement.

r005.rationale: It does not call for research into deeper test-time learning or adaptation.

astra-6.text:
For me, the most convincing thing would be a system that can learn to do something we didn’t explicitly train it to do. You give it a new problem, it tries an approach, realizes what it got wrong, and gets better from that experience. And it can do that across domains, without us having to go back and build a new training pipeline each time.

I don’t think one benchmark would convince me. I’d want to see it operate over time: can it work through a genuinely unfamiliar problem, recognize when it needs help, and carry what it learns into the next problem? That would be much stronger evidence to me than a spectacular answer to a single question.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning from experience without a new training pipeline, but does not define AGI as improving itself without any human involvement; it even mentions recognizing when it needs help.

r002.rationale: It does not identify improving AI models as economically valuable work.

r003.rationale: It does not compare human–LLM collaboration with LLMs operating without humans.

r004.rationale: It makes no judgment about the 2024 and early 2025 AI development trajectory.

r005.rationale: It describes learning and adaptation as evidence for AGI, but does not call for research into them as a means of enabling models to improve themselves without human involvement.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the most convincing thing would be a system that can learn something genuinely new—something we didn’t anticipate when we trained it—and then use that knowledge to solve problems in the real world. It shouldn’t need us to carefully frame every task or guide every step. It should be able to try things, recognize when it’s wrong, and improve. If it could do that reliably across a broad range of work, I’d take that as very strong evidence.

r001.rationale: The response says a system should learn, try things, and improve without being guided at every step, but it does not define AGI as self-improvement without any human involvement.

r003.rationale: It does not compare human–LLM collaboration with LLMs operating without humans.
